explanation: Business intelligence tool proficiency is the ability to use enterprise platforms such as Power BI, Tableau, or SAS Visual Analytics to systematically discover, assess, and compare internal, administrative, and alternative data sources. In future work, analysts will use these tools to support automated scanning, suitability screening, cost-benefit and risk analysis, and clear documentation of why new data collection is or is not required. This capability also supports reusable, auditable, and digitally enabled workflows aligned with enterprise standards.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and Statcan 2030 Future Slide requires needs identification and data availability assessment to be digital-first, enterprise-wide, and evidence-based. The change drivers point to greater use of automation, metadata-assisted discovery, reuse of standardized components, and stronger justification before launching new surveys, which directly increases the need for proficiency in business intelligence tools. Without this capability, staff cannot meet the expected future requirements for rapid scanning, transparent decision-making, and auditable analysis across GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.5, and 3.2.

explanation: Digital Cost-Benefit and Risk Assessment is the capability to systematically evaluate existing, administrative, alternative, and new data collection options using digital tools, standardized metadata, and enterprise business intelligence platforms. It enables staff to compare cost, risk, suitability, reusability, and automation feasibility early in the process, so decisions on whether to launch new surveys or use other sources are evidence-based, auditable, and aligned with digital-first design and processing requirements.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires formalized, up-front assessment of data availability, cost, risk, and automation potential before new initiatives proceed. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5, these change drivers shift work toward enterprise scanning of data assets, documented business cases for new collection, and machine-actionable, reusable process design, making digital cost-benefit and risk assessment essential to determining and justifying future work requirements.

skill_gap: Data Source Evaluation for Automation Potential
explanation: This capability is the ability to systematically assess internal, administrative, alternative, and new data sources to determine whether they are suitable for automated, reusable, and digitally enabled statistical solutions. It requires analysts to use enterprise business intelligence and metadata-driven tools to scan data availability, evaluate quality, legal/privacy and risk considerations, and document evidence-based decisions on whether existing sources can meet needs before proposing new collection. It also supports ongoing evaluation by linking source selection decisions to automated monitoring, performance dashboards, and continuous improvement processes.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively push the organization toward digital-first, efficient, and reusable solutions rather than defaulting to new surveys. These drivers increase the need for staff to assess automation potential, cost-benefit, risk, and strategic fit at the needs identification and data availability stages, while ensuring decisions are documented for transparent evaluation and continuous monitoring. As future work becomes more automated, metadata-enabled, and enterprise-coordinated, this capability directly determines whether analysts can meet requirements for rapid triage, evidence-based justification, and exception-based survey design.

explanation: Cross-disciplinary collaboration is the ability to work effectively with IT, automation, metadata, and operational specialists to assess data needs, evaluate existing sources, and shape new initiatives from the earliest stages. In future work, this capability supports digitally enabled needs identification, automated data availability and suitability assessment, and the design of machine-actionable, reusable processing and analysis workflows that align with enterprise standards.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state requirements in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to more integrated, digital-first, and automation-enabled ways of working across the statistical production process. These change drivers influence work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5 by requiring staff to collaborate early with IT and automation specialists to use enterprise discovery tools, document evidence-based business cases, assess legal/privacy/risk considerations, and design standardized, metadata-driven solutions rather than relying only on traditional subject-matter assessment.

explanation: This capability is the ability to create clear, digital, audit-ready justification for new data collection or data-source augmentation by systematically assessing existing internal, administrative, and alternative data first. It requires analysts to use enterprise discovery and business intelligence tools, document stakeholder engagement, and produce evidence-based business cases grounded in cost-benefit, risk, suitability, and automation considerations across needs identification, data availability assessment, and business case preparation.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 requires staff to formally document why new collection is necessary only after automated, enterprise-wide scans and suitability assessments of existing and alternative sources have been completed. This is directly driven by Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-first operations, reuse of existing data, transparency, automation, and faster evidence-based decision-making, thereby making audit-ready justification a core requirement for future work.

explanation: Digital Asset Discovery and Prioritization is the capability to systematically find, assess, and rank existing data assets, metadata, and automated solutions before proposing new collection. It supports early-stage strategy, needs identification, concept development, and data suitability assessment by using standardized discovery tools, metadata, and evidence-based criteria such as scalability, reusability, feasibility, cost, and strategic fit. This capability helps ensure new surveys or bespoke collection are pursued only when existing digital assets are demonstrably insufficient.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward digital-first, efficient, and reusable approaches to meeting information needs. These change drivers influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5 by requiring staff to scan internal, administrative, and alternative data first, use metadata- and AI-enabled discovery tools, prioritize automation-compatible options, and provide clear evidence when new collection is necessary.

explanation: Metadata-assisted data source discovery is the capability to use standardized metadata, discovery platforms, and automated screening tools to quickly find, classify, and assess internal, administrative, alternative, and external data sources before considering new collection. It supports enterprise-wide needs identification, concept alignment, and data availability assessment by enabling documented scans, digital feasibility checks, suitability scoring, and compatibility reviews that feed downstream automation and auditability.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires staff to default to existing data, document enterprise scans, and assess automation, risk, resource implications, and digital compatibility before development, procurement, or new surveys proceed. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5, these change drivers shift work toward automated discovery, standardized metadata, FAIR-aligned inventories, and evidence-based justification for new collection, making metadata-assisted discovery essential to meeting future operational requirements.

explanation: Digital Feasibility Documentation is the capability to assess and clearly document whether proposed procurement, program changes, or new data collection are compatible with enterprise digital standards, existing data assets, automation opportunities, and resource and risk constraints. It supports early-stage decision-making by requiring staff to complete enterprise scans, feasibility checks, and evidence-based business cases before proceeding with custom development, surveys, or dissemination solutions, ensuring work is reusable, auditable, and aligned with standardized digital platforms.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires explicit digital feasibility, cost-benefit, and reuse documentation before new collection, development, or procurement decisions are approved. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 3.3, these change drivers shift work toward enterprise-wide scanning of existing data and tools, automated suitability assessment, and modular platform-based delivery, making documented digital compatibility, automation readiness, and justification for exceptions essential future workforce requirements.

explanation: Digital stakeholder engagement is the capability to consult, assess needs, and build consensus with partners through online platforms, metadata-enabled tools, dashboards, and digital feedback channels. In practice, it supports faster, more transparent interactions across needs identification, needs confirmation, and product promotion by enabling staff to navigate digital environments, manage feedback, document decisions, and guide stakeholders through trade-offs using data-driven evidence.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to a more digital, agile, and AI-enabled operating model in which stakeholder interactions increasingly occur through platforms, APIs, and automated channels. These drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 7.4 by requiring staff to identify and confirm needs through metadata and discovery tools, support cost-benefit and prioritization discussions digitally, and promote products through integrated digital ecosystems with real-time engagement tracking.

explanation: Data Asset Discovery & Platform Navigation is the capability to use collaborative data discovery platforms to quickly locate, assess, and explain existing data assets using machine-actionable metadata. It includes guiding stakeholders through real-time suitability, feasibility, legal, privacy, and quality considerations so decisions about reuse, concept alignment, or the need for new collection can be made quickly and transparently.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a future model centred on reuse-first decision-making, digital service delivery, and greater use of integrated data, metadata, and automation. Those change drivers directly influence work in GSBPM 1.2, 1.4, and 1.5 by requiring staff to consult through platform-based tools, validate concepts against standardized inventories, and assess data availability through automated discovery and suitability screening—capabilities not covered by the current subject-matter advisory focus.

explanation: Cost-Benefit Analysis for Data Reuse is the capability to assess whether stakeholder needs can be met through existing internal, administrative, or alternative data before proposing new collection, and to clearly explain the trade-offs in cost, timeliness, quality, feasibility, and respondent burden. In future work, this capability supports analysts in using automated data discovery and metadata platforms during needs identification, consultation, and data availability assessment to make transparent, evidence-based recommendations on fit-for-use and when new surveys are truly necessary.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide emphasizes digital service delivery, greater reuse of existing data, reduced response burden, and more efficient, transparent decision-making. These change drivers directly influence GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to use automated discovery tools, apply explicit cost-benefit and feasibility criteria, and justify any new collection with strong evidence that no suitable reusable data source exists.

explanation: This capability enables employees to lead fast-paced analytics discussions with stakeholders, using metadata platforms, dashboards, and suitability assessments to jointly evaluate available data sources and translate diverse perspectives into clear, actionable recommendations. It supports future work in needs confirmation, data availability assessment, and processing/analysis design by combining stakeholder facilitation with agile decision-making, trade-off analysis, and collaboration across business, methodological, and technical teams.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to faster, more platform-enabled, and evidence-driven decisions about whether existing administrative or alternative data can meet emerging needs before launching new collection. Across GSBPM 1.2, 1.5, and 2.5, these change drivers increase the need for staff who can facilitate iterative stakeholder sessions, assess fit-for-use and operational impacts in real time, and integrate feedback into reusable, auditable, and machine-actionable analytical designs.

explanation: Machine-Actionable Metadata Interpretation is the ability to read and apply standardized, machine-readable metadata to quickly determine whether a data asset is relevant, usable, and compliant for a specific analytical purpose. In practice, this capability supports automated data discovery, concept alignment, and metadata-driven processing design by enabling staff to validate fit-for-use, interpret quality and legal context, and make sound decisions in platform-enabled, high-throughput environments.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and StatCan 2030 Future State shifts source assessment, concept identification, and processing design toward automated discovery, FAIR metadata, and machine-actionable decision rules, especially in GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 2.5. It is also reinforced by Mandate letter expectations to modernize service delivery and use data more effectively, requiring employees to interpret machine-actionable metadata so they can assess administrative and alternative data sources rapidly, justify when new surveys are necessary, and support auditable, reusable, platform-based workflows.

explanation: Platform-Assisted Feasibility Assessment is the capability to use automated data discovery, metadata, and decision-support platforms to quickly determine whether stakeholder needs can be met through existing sources and to clearly communicate the trade-offs involved. It supports faster, more transparent consultations by helping employees assess reuse options, suitability, timeliness, cost-benefit, and operational impacts before recommending new collection or development work. This capability is especially important in needs confirmation, data availability assessment, and reuse of standardized dissemination components, where platform navigation, evidence-based judgment, and stakeholder dialogue are increasingly central.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a future operating model centered on reuse, modernization, automation, and more efficient delivery through enterprise platforms rather than defaulting to new surveys or custom builds. These change drivers directly influence future work requirements in GSBPM 1.2, 1.5, and 3.3 by requiring employees to use machine-actionable metadata, automated suitability screening, and standardized corporate tools to make explicit feasibility and cost-benefit decisions, justify exceptions, and support stakeholder outcomes with greater speed, consistency, and transparency.

explanation: Administrative/Alternative Data Integration is the capability to find, assess, and adapt existing administrative or alternative data sources using metadata-driven platforms instead of defaulting to new bespoke collection. It supports future work in identifying needs, checking data availability and suitability, and integrating data by enabling rapid source discovery, suitability screening, reusable integration, and exception-based human oversight within auditable, standardized workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to a stronger requirement to reuse existing data, reduce unnecessary survey collection, and operate through digital, interoperable, and automated platforms. Those drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 5.1 by making metadata-assisted discovery, evidence-based justification for new collection, and rapid integration of administrative and alternative data core requirements, whereas the current model is still oriented toward bespoke procurement and manual assessment.

skill_gap: Data Discovery Platform and Metadata Tool Use
explanation: This capability is the ability to use real-time data discovery platforms, metadata standards, and automated assessment tools to quickly find, evaluate, and reuse data sources. It supports future work where concept identification, data availability checks, and data integration are increasingly automated, metadata-driven, and aligned with FAIR principles, with staff focusing more on validating results, managing exceptions, and curating metadata than on manual source review.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point to faster, more integrated, and more automated use of existing data before launching new collection. Those change drivers increase the need for machine-actionable metadata, automated suitability screening, and interoperable discovery and integration tools across GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 5.1, while the current workforce remains oriented to databases and program-level expertise rather than real-time discovery and automated metadata analysis.

skill_gap: Automated Suitability Scoring and Metadata Standards
explanation: This capability enables analysts to interpret metadata-driven automated suitability scores, understand how AI-based assessments were produced, and judge their strengths, weaknesses, and limitations. As work shifts from manually assessing data sources to overseeing automated discovery and scoring, analysts must manage exceptions, validate legal, privacy, quality, and fairness considerations, and explain automated outputs in a clear, evidence-based way. It also supports the design and use of machine-actionable, FAIR-aligned metadata and standardized automated workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to more automated, metadata-driven, and AI-enabled statistical operations that reduce manual assessment and increase the need for human oversight. These drivers influence future work requirements in GSBPM 1.5, 2.5, and 6.3 by making automated suitability screening, machine-actionable design, and AI-supported interpretation central to the role, while reserving human effort for exception management, legal and ethical review, and trusted communication of results.

skill_gap: Risk Assessment and Legal Vetting Frameworks
explanation: This capability is the ability to assess legal, privacy, governance, and compliance risks when automated tools identify or score potential data sources and analytical outputs. As work shifts under GSBPM 1.5, 2.5, and 6.3 from manual assessment to automated suitability screening and AI-enabled workflows, analysts must focus on human oversight, exception handling, legal vetting, and interpreting high-risk or novel cases before data is acquired or used.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Departmental Plan and StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to more automated, metadata-driven, and AI-supported data discovery, processing, and interpretation, while mandate-letter expectations reinforce the need to maintain public trust, privacy, and responsible data use. Together, these change drivers shift future work away from routine source assessment toward edge-case review, compliance validation, and strategic negotiation on new data sources, making strong risk assessment and legal vetting capability essential.

explanation: This capability involves negotiating and managing partnerships to secure access to new and diverse data sources when automated discovery and suitability tools cannot resolve complex cases. As work shifts toward supervising automated suitability scoring systems, employees must focus on exception management, legal and ethical review, and strategic discussions with external data owners while clearly interpreting constraints, trade-offs, and opportunities for stakeholders.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of administrative, alternative, and external data, stronger digital and AI-enabled processes, and more strategic collaboration to meet emerging information needs. These change drivers influence future work in GSBPM 1.2, 1.5, and 6.3 by automating routine data discovery and assessment, which increases the importance of human capability in negotiating access agreements, managing high-risk or novel partnerships, and explaining legal, quality, and ethical implications in complex stakeholder environments.

skill_gap: Critical Assessment of Automated Data Source Reports
explanation: This capability is the ability to review automated data source suitability reports with informed professional judgment, not simply accept system outputs at face value. As data availability checks, needs identification, and output interpretation become increasingly automated, employees must assess the quality, relevance, limitations, and contextual fit of automated recommendations, especially in complex, novel, or high-risk cases. They must also clearly justify when automated findings support or do not support proceeding to new survey design.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of automation, AI, administrative data, and evidence-based decision making before launching new surveys. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 6.3 by making automated discovery, suitability screening, and AI-generated outputs central to operations, which increases the need for analysts who can critically interpret, validate, and challenge system recommendations while explaining their methodological, ethical, and practical limits.

skill_gap: Partnership Management and Complex Stakeholder Engagement
explanation: This capability is the ability to build and manage strategic relationships with diverse data holders and stakeholders, and to negotiate access, terms, and ongoing collaboration in increasingly complex data environments. As needs identification, consultation, and data availability assessment become more automated through metadata platforms and AI-supported discovery, human effort shifts toward handling complex cases, legal and ethical considerations, procurement discussions, and sustained relationship management with new partners.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point to greater use of administrative, alternative, and externally sourced data, supported by digital platforms, automation, and AI-enabled decision processes. These change drivers reshape work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by reducing routine source discovery and increasing the need for staff who can manage strategic partnerships, negotiate rights and access, and guide complex stakeholder engagement when new data sources must be secured and governed.

explanation: Domain-Driven Intervention Capability is the ability to apply economic theory, statistical methods, and contextual judgement to determine when automated assessments, edits, or analytical outputs need human review or override. As processing, editing, and interpretation become more AI-enabled across activities 2.5, 5.4, and 6.3, this capability ensures staff can validate algorithmic results, manage complex exceptions, and explain outputs in ways that are methodologically sound, ethical, and relevant to users.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of automation, AI-enabled workflows, faster insight generation, and stronger expectations for trust, transparency, and responsible data use. These change drivers directly influence future work requirements by shifting staff responsibilities from manual processing to oversight of automated pipelines, exception handling, fairness and quality assessment, and context-sensitive interpretation where domain expertise is essential to judge when system outputs are insufficient or inappropriate.

explanation: Complex Edge-case Resolution is the capability to step in when automated data discovery, suitability screening, and AI-supported evaluation cannot produce a clear or acceptable answer. It enables analysts to resolve unprecedented data suitability disputes, legal or ethical conflicts, and partner-related issues, while interpreting system-generated signals and explaining decisions in a transparent, evidence-based way.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward more automated, metadata-driven, and AI-enabled statistical operations, which shifts human work away from routine assessment and toward exceptional, high-risk cases. Across GSBPM 1.5, 6.3, and 8.2, these change drivers increase the need for analysts who can resolve cases outside automated boundaries, apply judgment to legal and ethical risks, interpret ambiguous outputs, and intervene when continuous monitoring identifies novel or complex issues.

explanation: AI Process Communication is the capability to translate AI-generated outputs, automated disclosure decisions, and process recommendations into clear, credible explanations for both technical and non-technical audiences. As analysis, disclosure control, and processing design become more automated, employees must focus on interpreting results in context, explaining risks, limitations, fairness, and methodology, and supporting negotiation and decision-making through strong narrative and oversight communication.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more digital, automated, transparent, and trusted statistical operations, which increases the need to explain AI-enabled processes and decisions to diverse stakeholders. These change drivers influence future work in GSBPM 6.3, 6.4, and 2.5 by shifting staff responsibilities from manual processing toward oversight, exception review, and communication of automated outputs, making clear interpretation, justification, and trust-building essential.

explanation: This capability is the ability to produce clear, concise, and evidence-based written rationales for business cases, output decisions, and evaluation recommendations in environments increasingly shaped by automation, reusable data sources, and legal or governance requirements. It includes translating automated assessments, cost-benefit and risk analyses, and stakeholder trade-offs into persuasive written justifications, vetoes, and negotiation correspondence that support faster, more transparent decision-making across activities such as establishing output objectives, submitting business cases, and conducting evaluations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires stronger written justification for decisions that prioritize administrative and alternative data, automation, enterprise platforms, and rapid governance review. Across GSBPM 1.3, 1.6, and 8.2, staff must now document why surveys are launched or avoided, explain evidence-based recommendations and vetoes using automated outputs and continuous evaluation signals, and negotiate trade-offs with stakeholders in ways that are transparent, legally sound, and aligned with strategic modernization drivers.

explanation: AI pipeline oversight is the capability to review, interpret, and validate outputs produced by AI-enabled sample selection, editing, imputation, and validation processes rather than manually building or correcting them. It includes monitoring automated and metadata-driven pipelines for quality, reproducibility, auditability, anomalies, and ethical risks, while applying human judgment to exceptions and explaining results in context.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts key activities such as 5.4 Edit and impute, 6.2 Validate outputs, and 6.3 Interpret and explain outputs from manual execution to AI-enabled, auditable, and metadata-driven pipelines requiring human oversight. It is also aligned with Mandate letters emphasizing responsible modernization, digital transformation, and trustworthy use of data and AI, which together increase the need for staff who can validate automated logic, interpret flagged issues, assure quality and ethics, and remain accountable for final outputs.

explanation: Administrative & alternative data integration is the capability to identify, assess, combine, and govern administrative, survey, and alternative data sources within standardized, metadata-driven statistical workflows. In future work, this means less manual data preparation and more oversight of automated integration pipelines, including validating suitability, configuring integration rules, ensuring provenance and quality, and reviewing AI-enabled outputs in context.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of administrative and alternative data, stronger interoperability and metadata standards, and more automated, AI-enabled production processes. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.5, 5.1, and 6.3 by requiring employees to assess data availability through automated discovery, manage auditable integration of multiple data sources, and critically interpret and validate outputs generated from those integrated pipelines.

explanation: Exception management in automated systems is the capability to identify when AI-enabled validation, editing, imputation, or analytical pipelines produce ambiguous, anomalous, or high-risk results and to apply professional judgement to resolve them appropriately. As work shifts from manual production to oversight of automated outputs, employees must be able to interpret flagged cases, conduct root-cause analysis, and make defensible decisions that preserve data quality, auditability, transparency, and ethical assurance across activities such as validating outputs, editing and imputing data, and interpreting results.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point toward greater use of automation, AI, administrative and alternative data, and modernized, metadata-driven production processes, which change employee roles from operational execution to oversight and assurance. Those change drivers directly influence future work requirements in GSBPM 5.4, 6.2, and 6.3 by increasing the need for staff to manage exceptions, troubleshoot automated outputs, assess fairness and explainability, and retain accountability for final quality when automated systems encounter complex or unclear cases.

explanation: This capability is the ability to work with metadata-driven statistical production and modular system design so that automated workflows, validation rules, and data integrations are standardized, auditable, and reusable. It supports a shift from manually building models toward configuring, reviewing, and validating AI-enabled processes, including assessing administrative and alternative data sources, applying FAIR principles, and ensuring ongoing quality control and interpretability of outputs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more automated, AI-enabled, and interoperable statistical operations that depend on metadata standards and modular frameworks. These change drivers directly influence work in GSBPM 2.5, 6.3, and 1.5 by requiring staff to design machine-actionable and reusable processes, oversee and explain AI-generated outputs, and use standardized metadata to assess and integrate data sources—capabilities not yet explicit in the current work description.

explanation: AI output interpretation and validation is the capability to review, question, and confirm AI-generated assessments of data source fitness, quality metrics, and validation results before they are used in production or decision-making. As review and validation work shifts from manual inspection to automated, auditable pipelines across GSBPM 5.3, 6.2, and 6.3, employees must interpret flagged exceptions, assess unclear or inconsistent outcomes, and explain the quality, methodological, and ethical limits of automated outputs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to increased use of AI-enabled, metadata-driven, and automated validation and analysis processes, while Mandate letters reinforce expectations for trustworthy, responsible, and transparent use of advanced digital tools in public service delivery. These change drivers directly shift work requirements from manual validation toward human oversight of automated decisions, requiring staff to validate AI outputs, interpret anomalies, and ensure fairness, auditability, and confidence in results where this is not currently part of decision-making requirements.
